## Week 2, Session 5 — Time series basics {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics}

<div class="callout callout-note">
**Inference lab** using the five-step template:
Hypothesis → Visualise → Assumptions → Conduct → Conclude.
</div>

### Learning objectives {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-learning-objectives}

- Decompose a seasonal time series into trend, seasonal, and
  residual components.
- Fit an ARIMA model automatically with `forecast::auto.arima`.
- Detect a mean shift using `changepoint::cpt.mean`.

### Prerequisites {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-prerequisites}

Regression; basic familiarity with the `ts` class.

### Background {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-background}

A time series differs from cross-sectional data in one crucial way:
observations close in time are correlated with one another, so
standard errors based on independence are wrong. Classical
decomposition splits a series into a slowly varying trend, a
periodic seasonal component, and a residual. ARIMA models capture
the residual autocorrelation with autoregressive and moving-average
terms, possibly after differencing to remove a unit root.

Change-point detection asks a different question: given a series,
when (if ever) did the underlying mean or variance shift? The
`changepoint` package implements several methods; `cpt.mean` with a
penalised likelihood criterion is a common starting point. In
epidemiology, change-points flag outbreaks, policy changes, and
data-collection transitions.

A seasonally adjusted series is not the same as a detrended series.
Seasonal adjustment removes only the regular period; detrending
removes the slow evolution. Most anomalies you care about (an
outbreak, an intervention) live in what remains.

### Setup {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-setup}

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(forecast)
library(changepoint)
set.seed(42)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

### 1. Hypothesis {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-1-hypothesis}

A simulated monthly series has a linear trend, a yearly seasonal
cycle, and a mean shift at month 80. Decomposition, ARIMA, and
change-point detection should each recover an interpretable piece.

### 2. Visualise {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-2-visualise}

```r
months <- 144
t  <- seq_len(months)
trend <- 0.08 * t
season <- 4 * sin(2 * pi * t / 12)
shift  <- if_else(t >= 80, 5, 0)
y      <- 20 + trend + season + shift + rnorm(months, 0, 1.5)
ts_y   <- ts(y, frequency = 12, start = c(2014, 1))

autoplot(ts_y) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Simulated rate")
```

### 3. Assumptions {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-3-assumptions}

STL decomposition assumes the seasonal period is fixed and known.
ARIMA assumes a linear, time-invariant generating process after
differencing. `cpt.mean` assumes the variance is approximately
constant — change-points in variance would need `cpt.var`.

### 4. Conduct {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-4-conduct}

```r
decomp <- stl(ts_y, s.window = "periodic")
autoplot(decomp)
```

```r
fit_arima <- auto.arima(ts_y)
fit_arima
```

```r
fc <- forecast(fit_arima, h = 12)
autoplot(fc) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Simulated rate")
```

```r
cpt <- cpt.mean(as.numeric(ts_y), method = "PELT")
cpts(cpt)
```

```r
tibble(t = t, y = as.numeric(ts_y)) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cpts(cpt), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Month index", y = "Rate")
```

### 5. Concluding statement {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-5-concluding-statement}

> STL cleanly separated a linear trend, a 12-month seasonal cycle,
> and a residual containing the simulated mean shift. `auto.arima`
> selected `fit_arima$arma |> paste(collapse = ", ")`
> (p, q, P, Q, frequency, d, D). PELT detected change-points at
> months `paste(cpts(cpt), collapse = ", ")`, close to the
> simulated truth of 80.


### Common pitfalls {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-common-pitfalls}

- Using daily ARIMA on weekly-seasonal data without telling the
  model the period.
- Calling every bump a change-point; penalise harder and re-run.
- Using `lm()` on a time series as if residuals were independent.
- Forecasting far beyond the observed period without widening the
  intervals in the report.

### Further reading {#sec-chapters-09-timeseries-labs-lab-time-series-basics-further-reading}

- Hyndman RJ, Athanasopoulos G. *Forecasting: Principles and
  Practice*.
- Killick R, Fearnhead P, Eckley IA (2012), *Optimal detection of
  changepoints with a linear computational cost*.
- Box GEP, Jenkins GM. *Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and
  Control*.
